question: In which part of the operations manual are the MEL, CDL and emergency evacuation procedures found?

options.text: Part C, routes, aerodromes and their minima

explanation: All type-related instructions, including abnormal and emergency procedures, the CDL, the MEL and evacuation procedures, are in Part B.

question: Up to what point may the MEL be used?

options.text: Until reaching cruising level after take-off
Up to the commencement of flight

explanation: The MEL applies up to the commencement of flight, which means it can be used during taxi until the aircraft starts moving under its own power to take off.

question: What is the "commencement of flight" for MEL purposes?

options.text: When it first moves under its own power to take off
When the wheels leave the runway on the take-off roll

explanation: Commencement of flight is the point when an aeroplane begins to move under its own power for the purpose of preparing to take off.

question: An airworthiness directive conflicts with the MEL. Which applies?
explanation: If there is a conflict between an airworthiness directive and the MEL, the airworthiness directive overrides.

question: What does "inoperative" mean for MEL purposes?

options.text: The item has passed its service life
The item has been removed for cleaning
A fault message has appeared on the maintenance computer
It does not do its job or stay within limits

explanation: Inoperative means the equipment does not accomplish its intended purpose or is not consistently within design tolerances. A fault message from a fault-tolerant system does not necessarily mean the equipment is inoperative.

question: How restrictive must an operator's MEL be compared with the MMEL?

options.text: It may ignore the MMEL with the chief pilot's approval
Less restrictive, to suit the operator

explanation: The MEL must be based on, and no less restrictive than, the master MEL accepted by the authority, and is approved by the authority.

question: Who decides whether to accept an aeroplane with defects allowed by the MEL or CDL?

options.text: The engineer who signs the release

explanation: The commander decides whether or not to accept an aeroplane with unserviceabilities allowed by the CDL or MEL.

question: Which three conditions are needed for ice to form on an airframe?

options.text: Liquid water, and air and airframe below 0 °C
Rain, warm air and a cold-soaked engine on the ground

explanation: Ice forms when liquid water is present, the ambient temperature is below 0 °C and the airframe temperature is below 0 °C.

question: What droplet size defines drizzle?

options.text: More than 0.5 mm in diameter and widely spaced
Less than 0.5 mm in diameter, very close together

explanation: Drizzle is fairly uniform precipitation of fine drops less than 0.5 mm in diameter, very close together. Rain drops are larger or more widely spaced.

question: Below what visibility is a water droplet suspension called fog?
explanation: Fog is a visible aggregate of minute water droplets reducing horizontal visibility at the surface to less than 1 km.

question: What is freezing fog?

options.text: Fog over frozen ground that does not affect aircraft
Supercooled fog that freezes on contact
Fog made of ice crystals only

explanation: Freezing fog consists of supercooled water droplets that freeze on contact with exposed objects, forming rime or clear ice.

question: How is frost (hoar frost) formed?

options.text: By supercooled cloud droplets freezing on the surface

explanation: Frost is a crystalline deposit formed by sublimation, when water vapour is deposited directly as ice on a surface below 0 °C.

question: What is slush?

options.text: Dry snow that can be blown
Snow so wet it splatters when stamped
Ice covered by a thin layer of standing water

explanation: Slush is water-saturated snow which splatters when hit with a heel-and-toe slap-down motion.

question: When is snow described as wet?

options.text: When it is more than 10 cm deep
When the temperature is well below freezing and the snow is powdery
When the ambient temperature is near or above freezing

explanation: Dry snow occurs when the temperature is below freezing; wet snow when it is near or above freezing.

question: What is the difference between de-icing and anti-icing?

options.text: De-icing prevents ice; anti-icing removes it
De-icing removes ice; anti-icing prevents it forming
De-icing is in flight only; anti-icing on the ground only

explanation: De-icing is removing ice from the airframe; anti-icing is preventing its formation for a period.

question: By how much can airframe ice reduce lift and increase drag?

options.text: Lift by up to 30% and drag up by up to 40%
Lift by up to 80% and drag up by up to 100%
It affects only drag, not lift
Lift by up to 5% and drag up by up to 5%

explanation: Ice alters the shape of flying surfaces; lift can be reduced by up to 30% and drag increased by up to 40%, raising stall speed and reducing control.

question: Which instrument problem can ice cause?

options.text: False air data from iced pitot or static ports
A brighter instrument display caused by ice crystals

explanation: Ice on pitot tubes, static vents or angle-of-attack vanes can cause false attitude, airspeed, angle-of-attack and power information.

question: Why may ice formed on the ground be more dangerous than the same amount formed in flight?

options.text: It only forms on the fuselage
Its effect can be completely different

explanation: Ice, frost and snow formed on critical surfaces on the ground can have a totally different effect on flight characteristics from ice formed in flight.

question: What is the "clean aircraft concept"?

options.text: Washing the aircraft before every flight
Removing all unnecessary equipment before take-off
Removing all unnecessary equipment and cargo before take-off
No take-off with frozen deposits on critical surfaces

explanation: Take-off shall not be attempted when ice, snow, slush or frost is present on or adhering to the wings, propellers, control surfaces, engine inlets or other critical surfaces.

question: Which of these is an approved method of ground de-icing?

options.text: Running the engines at high power
Hot air blowers warming the airframe
Pouring cold water over the wings

explanation: Approved methods include de-icing fluids (including taxi-through systems), hot air blowers and manual sweeping of frost and light ice.

question: What is a one-step de-icing/anti-icing procedure?

options.text: De-icing and anti-icing in one go, one fluid
De-icing followed later by anti-icing with a different fluid
Anti-icing only, without removing the ice
De-icing only, with no protection afterwards

explanation: In a one-step procedure de-icing and anti-icing are done at the same time with a combined fluid. A two-step procedure removes ice first and then applies anti-icing fluid.

question: What is holdover time?

options.text: The time before the engines can be started
The time spent in the de-icing bay
How long the fluid stays effective
The time the fluid takes to dry completely

explanation: Holdover time is the estimated time during which the fluid remains effective; the take-off roll must start within it, otherwise the treatment must be repeated.

question: The holdover time is exceeded before take-off. What must happen?

options.text: The crew may take off if the wings look clear
The de-icing and anti-icing must be repeated
The crew may take off within 5 more minutes
The crew must cancel the flight

explanation: The aircraft must start its take-off roll within the HOT, or the whole process must be repeated.

question: On which factors does holdover time depend?

options.text: Only the runway length and the aircraft's take-off mass
OAT, skin temperature, precipitation, wind and fluid

explanation: HOT depends on outside air temperature, skin temperature, type of precipitation, wind, and the type and concentration of fluid.

question: Which de-icing fluid types are generally used for turbojet aircraft?
explanation: Types I, II and IV are in general use for turbojet aircraft; Type III is suited to slower aircraft such as turboprops.

question: How must an aircraft be treated with de-icing fluid?

options.text: On the upper wing surfaces only
On one wing at a time with a flight in between
Only on the side facing the wind

explanation: Aircraft must be treated symmetrically.

question: When should the pre-take-off check for contamination be made?

options.text: After take-off, by looking at the wing from the cabin window
As late as possible, usually from the cabin
At the stand before pushback only

explanation: The commander must ensure critical surfaces are clear just before take-off; the check is made as close to take-off as possible, normally by looking at the wings from inside.

question: Where are known bird migration routes and times published?

options.text: In the AIP, en route section

explanation: Bird concentration areas are marked on charts, and migration routes and times are published in the AIP en route section.

question: When is the risk from bird strikes highest?

options.text: In the hold at high level
Over the open ocean at night, far from land
Near the ground, at take-off and landing

explanation: The highest risk is close to the ground, during take-off and landing, when deviating from the flight path is impractical and power settings are critical.

question: Which aerodromes are most vulnerable to bird strikes?

options.text: Those with long runways and large aprons
Those near coasts and natural bird habitats

explanation: Aerodromes close to coastal areas and natural habitats are the most vulnerable.

question: Which of these is an example of incompatible land use near an airport because it attracts birds?

options.text: A car factory with a flat roof
A rubbish dump or landfill site

explanation: Land uses that attract birds include fish processing, agriculture, cattle feed lots, rubbish dumps and landfill, wildlife refuges, lakes, golf courses and slaughterhouses (and in some cases roofs, car parks and food outlets).

question: What must a pilot do on seeing a potential bird hazard?

options.text: Report it to the ground station
Report it to the operator after landing only
Note it in the journey log only

explanation: Pilots are required to report a potential bird hazard to the appropriate ground station, so other aircraft can be warned.

question: What may an airport set up where birds are a continual risk?

options.text: A no-fly zone for all aircraft

explanation: Where birds are a continual risk, airports set up bird control units using trained staff and techniques to reduce birds on the aerodrome.

question: Which of these is a method of noise abatement?

options.text: Using reverse thrust in the air
Banning all night flights at every aerodrome everywhere

explanation: Noise abatement uses noise preferential runways, noise preferential routes and noise abatement take-off or approach procedures.

question: When noise abatement and safety conflict, which has priority?
explanation: The operator must ensure safety has priority over noise abatement.

question: How many departure procedures must an operator define for each aeroplane type?
explanation: For each type two departure procedures are defined: NADP 1 for the close-in objective and NADP 2 for the distant objective.

question: Which noise abatement departure procedure reduces noise close to the aerodrome?
explanation: NADP 1 is designed to meet the close-in noise abatement objective; NADP 2 the distant objective.

question: Below which height must a noise abatement procedure not be started?
explanation: Noise abatement procedures shall not be executed below 240 m (800 ft) above aerodrome elevation.

question: In NADP 1, what is done at 800 ft?

options.text: Flaps are retracted at once and the aircraft accelerates to clean speed
The aircraft levels off until 3000 ft
Full power is kept and the aircraft accelerates
Power cut at 800 ft, take-off flap, V2 + 10–20 kt

explanation: In NADP 1, power is reduced at or above 800 ft and the aircraft climbs at V2 + 10–20 kt with take-off flap until 3000 ft, then accelerates and retracts flaps.

question: In NADP 2, what happens after 800 ft?

options.text: The aircraft keeps take-off flap and V2 + 20 kt to 3000 ft
Accelerate and retract flaps, cutting power as they retract
The aircraft levels off and holds

explanation: In NADP 2, not before 800 ft, the aircraft accelerates towards zero-flap speed, reducing power as flap retraction starts (or after it), then climbs at VZF + 10–20 kt to 3000 ft.

question: What is the initial climb speed up to the noise abatement initiation point?
explanation: The initial climb speed to the noise abatement initiation point shall not be less than V2 + 10 to 20 kt.

question: Up to what height do the example noise abatement climb procedures apply?
explanation: The example procedures run from 800 ft to 900 m (3000 ft), then the aircraft transitions to en route climb.

question: Should an operator use the same noise abatement procedure for a type at all aerodromes?

options.text: No, a different one for each aerodrome

explanation: The procedure specified for an aeroplane type should be the same for all aerodromes, with no more than two procedures per type.

question: An engine fails during a noise abatement departure. What power should be used?

options.text: Idle on the failed side and climb power on the other
Reduced power to keep noise low
The noise abatement power until 3000 ft
Pilot's choice; noise rules no longer apply

explanation: After an engine failure or other loss of performance, power settings are at the pilot's discretion and noise abatement considerations no longer apply.

question: When should noise abatement procedures not be used on departure?

options.text: When the aircraft is lightly loaded

explanation: Procedures are not to be used where a windshear warning exists or windshear or downburst activity is suspected.

question: Who may decide not to fly a noise abatement procedure if it cannot be done safely?
explanation: The pilot-in-command has the authority not to execute a procedure if conditions preclude its safe execution.

question: Which State approves an operator's noise abatement flight procedures?

options.text: The State of Registry of the engines
The State where the aerodrome is

explanation: The aerodrome's State ensures noise abatement objectives are specified; the State of the Operator approves the safe flight procedures developed by the operator.

question: Noise abatement should not decide the runway when the crosswind component, including gusts, exceeds what?
explanation: Noise abatement should not determine runway selection if the crosswind including gusts exceeds 15 kt (28 km/h).

question: Noise abatement should not decide the runway when the tailwind component, including gusts, exceeds what?
explanation: The tailwind limit is 5 kt (9 km/h) including gusts.

question: For landing, below what ceiling should noise abatement not decide the runway?
explanation: Noise abatement should not decide the landing runway when the ceiling is lower than 150 m (500 ft) above aerodrome elevation.

question: Below what visibility should noise abatement not decide the runway?
explanation: Noise abatement should not decide runway selection when horizontal visibility is less than 1.9 km (1900 m).

question: Which landing aid should normally be available on a noise preferential landing runway?

options.text: A runway at least 3000 m long
A rapid exit taxiway near the touchdown zone
Glide path guidance (ILS or slope lights)
A taxiway parallel to the runway

explanation: Runways should not normally be selected for landing unless they have suitable glide path guidance, such as ILS or a VASI (in VMC).

question: On a noise preferential route, above what height may turns after take-off be required?

options.text: 1500 ft above the aerodrome elevation only

explanation: Turns should not be required unless the aeroplane has reached, and can maintain throughout, a height of not less than 150 m (500 ft) above terrain and obstacles.

question: What bank angle limit normally applies to turns after take-off on noise routes?
explanation: The bank angle for turns after take-off is limited to 15°, unless an acceleration phase allows safe speeds for greater bank.

question: Should a turn coincide with a power reduction for noise abatement?
explanation: No turns should be required at the same time as a power reduction associated with a noise abatement procedure.

question: When may an aircraft be diverted from its noise preferential route?

options.text: Whenever the crew wish to save fuel or time
Above the noise height limit, or for safety

explanation: An aeroplane shall not be diverted from its route unless it has reached the upper limit for noise abatement or it is necessary for safety.

subtopic: Noise abatement on approach and landing
question: By what point must the aircraft be in the final landing configuration on a noise abatement approach?

options.text: The final approach fix only, whatever its distance
Outer marker or 5 NM, whichever comes first

explanation: The aircraft must be in the final landing configuration from the outer marker or 5 NM from the threshold, whichever is earlier.

subtopic: Noise abatement on approach and landing
question: Above what angle should a noise abatement approach not normally require descent?

options.text: 3°, unless the ILS glide path is steeper

explanation: Approaches should not be above the ILS glide path, the visual slope indicator, the normal PAR angle, or 3° unless the ILS requires more.

subtopic: Noise abatement on approach and landing
question: What do reduced power/reduced drag approach techniques involve?

options.text: Flying the whole approach with full flap
Flying the approach at idle with gear up to touchdown

explanation: These techniques delay extending flaps and gear until the final stages, giving uninterrupted descents at reduced power, with higher than normal gear and flap speeds.

subtopic: Noise abatement on approach and landing
question: Do noise abatement procedures prevent the use of reverse thrust on landing?

options.text: Only on runways longer than 3000 m

explanation: Noise abatement procedures do not prevent the use of reverse thrust on landing.

subtopic: Noise abatement on approach and landing
question: When may a displaced threshold be used for noise abatement?

options.text: Only if it really helps and enough runway remains
Always, at the operator's choice, whatever the runway length

explanation: A displaced threshold is only used for noise abatement if noise is sufficiently reduced and the remaining runway distance meets all requirements.

question: What descent gradient is typical for a CDFA profile?
explanation: A CDFA typically uses about 300 ft per NM, roughly a 3° path, maintained to the threshold without a level segment.

question: What is an advantage of the CDFA profile?

options.text: No need for a missed approach procedure
Fewer power changes and less fuel

explanation: CDFA minimises power changes, removes the level segment, supports a stabilised approach and saves fuel.
